title: Building An Enhanced Flight Mill for the Study of Tethered Insect Flight
author: Anastasia Bernat
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.bteznjf6
materials: Build the Flight Mill in a Makerspace

Download and install a 3D printing slicing software to convert .stl files to a 3D printer readable .gx file. Refer to the Table of Materials to download the free software program. NOTE: Other conversion software programs are acceptable, but this protocol assumes the makerspace is using the 3D printer and printing slicing software as referenced in the Table of Materials .
Double-click the icon of the 3D printing slicing software to start the software. Click Print > Machine Type and select the 3D printer that is located in the makerspace.

Discussion The simple, modern flight mill provides a range of advantages for researchers interested in studying tethered insect flight by delivering a reliable and automated design that tests multiple insects efficiently and cost-effectively 13, 31, 35 . Likewise, there is a strong incentive for researchers to adopt fast-emerging technologies and techniques from industry and other scientific fields as a means to build experimental tools to study ecological systems 9, 32, 33 . This protocol takes advantage of two rapidly emerging technologies, the 3D printer and the laser cutter, which are becoming increasingly available in communal makerspaces, in order to enhance the simple, modern flight mill. These enhancements provide a more flexible, adjustable, and collapsible design that accommodates insects of different sizes, minimizes stress placed on the insect, and allows the flight mill to be transported easily to multiple locations or environments. Furthermore, the additional expenses of using the technologies are minimal or even free. However, these technologies can also be a challenge to experiment with if reaching proficiency in using vector graphics editors and 3D image software is not readily available. In turn, the flight mill presented here serves to both encourage researchers to incorporate available emerging technologies in their workflow and to allow researchers to build a customizable, flexible, and effective flight mill without specialized knowledge of electronics, programming, or CAD models. The strongest aspects of this protocol are the makerspace's technologies that expand a user's flight mill design options, the use of magnetic paint to minimize insect stress, and the automation of flight recordings that processes multiple insects within a single recording. The laser cutter offers precise and exact cutting capabilities that can handle jobs of almost any complexity. The user can modify the acrylic support structure to mount additional 3D prints or purchased items. The 3D printer allows the user to create customizable flight mill components that can bypass costly, pre-made products with narrowly adjustable dimensions. 3D prints not proposed in this paper can also be built, such as landing platforms, supports that can quickly exchange between magnetic bearings and ball bearings, or even a new attachment that tethers an insect. Finally, the use of automated recording software and Python scripts to differentiate multiple flight trials within a single recording makes it possible to study sporadic bouts of flight to very long bouts of flight. However, given how variable flight activity and duration is across species, it is suggested that the user conducts preliminary trials in order to understand the limits and general patterns of a species' flight behavior so as to optimize data collection. The user can also assess the integrity of their recordings using the diagnostic heatmap(s) and can account for any necessary speed corrections in the scripts. Researchers should also be aware of the flight mill's general constraints. Previous studies have made known and have attempted to remediate the limitations of tethered flight, including a lack of tarsal contact to allow the insect to rest at will 18, 31 , the absence of energy expended when an insect takes-off 34 , the additional drag the insect overcomes when pushing the flight mill arm, and the insect needing to compensate for the outward aerodynamic forces experienced due to the centrifugal acceleration of its circular flight track 6, 35 . Additionally, there continue to be inconsistencies on how to categorize or more precisely quantify the short or 'trivial' bursts insects display, especially when comparing the flight behavior and mechanisms of large migratory insects to those of small insects who exhibit mostly hovering flight 24, 36, 37 . Despite these limitations, there has been significant progress in capturing and categorizing flight behavior within insect species, and researchers have continued to couple the flight mill with other technologies and methods 6, 7, 8 . The makerspace as a location of creativity, collaboration, and low barriers will further inspire researchers to troubleshoot 3D print design limitations or laser cut more intricate designs. Studies have surveyed the effectiveness of makerspaces not just as iterative product-making spaces but also as places of accelerated learning 10, 11, 12 . Engineering students overall scored higher in design comprehension, design documentation, and model quality when their designs were made using makerspace technology 11 . Additionally, their model development time dropped by 50%, indicating that makerspace exploration outperformed traditional rote theory and application coursework 11 . In turn, researchers with little design knowledge will be able to deepen it, and researchers who are also educators can take advantage of this space as a means to increase design organization, craftmanship, and technical dexterity for students. In a discipline like ecology that already makes use of a variety of tools for field and laboratory work, researchers can also develop, share, and standardize novel or enhanced tools. The flight mill proposed in this paper is only the start of what could be an approach to democratizing and rapidly spreading new means of collecting data. Flight mills have played an important role in enabling researchers to understand the dispersal of insects - an ecological phenomenon still essentially intractable in the field. Future advances in the design and application of the flight mill can be achieved as researchers become more proficient in emerging technologies and the software accompanying those technologies. This could include designing flight mill arm bearings that allow vertical lift or give the insect greater flight orientation flexibility. Additionally, the precision of laser cutters and 3D printers may be necessary for researchers interested in scaling down and calibrating for small insects with mostly hovering capabilities. In turn, the goal of this protocol was to provide an easy entry to these technologies while constructing one of the most common and useful devices in the field of behavioral ecology - the flight mill. If researchers have access to a communal makerspace and are committed to navigating its technologies, the resulting enhancements and improvements of the modern flight mill will lead to creative and collaborative flight mill design and will continue to offer insights into the underlying traits and mechanisms that influence insect species' variations and patterns in movement.

steps.title: Cut acrylic support sheets
steps.instruction: Cut eight transparent acrylic sheets (304.8 mm × 609.6 mm × 3.175 mm) on a laser cutter; do not use polycarbonate.

substeps.instruction: Create a vector file (AI, DXF or SVG) in Illustrator, Inkscape or similar with the designs for the outside vertical walls, central vertical wall and five horizontal shelves.
Draw cut lines in RGB Red (255,0,0) with a stroke width of 0.0001 pt and etch lines in RGB Blue (0,0,255) with the same stroke width.
Save the file and open it in the laser‑cutter software; verify that cut lines appear red and etch lines appear blue.
Set the material to Plastic → Acrylic, enter the measured sheet thickness (use a caliper), enable Z‑axis auto‑focus, set Figure Type to None and Intensity to 0 %.
Adjust laser % Power and % Speed based on a kerf‑key test (see step 2).
Follow makerspace safety rules, start the cut, and after cutting clean the cavity of excess material.

steps.title: Determine laser kerf
steps.instruction: Measure the laser kerf and adjust design dimensions accordingly.

substeps.instruction: Laser‑cut a kerf‑key (a 20 mm wide rectangular piece) and a matching slot.
Fit the key into the slot; record the slot width that holds the key most securely (e.g., 19.5 mm).
Calculate kerf = key width – slot width (e.g., 20 mm – 19.5 mm = 0.5 mm) and apply this offset to all slit and hole dimensions in the design.

steps.title: Assemble acrylic frame
steps.instruction: Insert the five horizontal shelves into the slits of the two outside vertical walls and the central vertical wall, aligning all holes.

steps.title: Prepare 3D‑print files
steps.instruction: Download the 3D_Prints.zip archive, unzip it to the desktop and import each STL into an online 3D‑modeling workspace.

substeps.instruction: Do not rotate objects along the Z‑axis; keep each within the 140 mm × 140 mm × 140 mm build volume.
For mirrored parts (linear guide rails), select the object, press M and choose the width‑axis mirror.

steps.title: 3D‑print components
steps.instruction: Print all listed parts in PLA with supports and raft enabled, using Standard resolution and the extruder temperature recommended by the printer guide.

substeps.instruction: Calibrate the extruder and verify sufficient filament.
Transfer each generated .gx file to the printer (USB or network) and start the print.
For each print, confirm proper filament adhesion to the build plate.

steps.title: List of 3D‑printed parts
steps.instruction: Print the following quantities and dimensions:

substeps.instruction: 8 linear guide rails – 100.05 mm × 23.50 mm × 7.00 mm
16 linear guide rail blocks – 22.08 mm × 11.47 mm × 12.47 mm
12–20 screws – 9.00 mm × 7.60 mm × 13.00 mm (use 3‑D printed screws where possible)
15 cross brackets – 50.00 mm × 50.00 mm × 20.00 mm
16 magnet holders – 12.75 mm × 12.50 mm × 15.75 mm
16 tube supports – 29.22 mm × 29.19 mm × 11.00 mm
16 short linear‑rail supports – 40.00 mm × 11.00 mm × 13.00 mm
16 long linear‑rail supports – 40.00 mm × 16.00 mm × 13.00 mm

steps.title: Attach neoprene to cross brackets
steps.instruction: Hot‑glue 3.175 mm‑thick neoprene sheets onto the interior walls of each cross bracket, let dry, then insert the brackets at the junctions of the acrylic shelves and walls.

steps.title: Install tube supports with 3‑D‑printed screws
steps.instruction: Screw each tube support onto the bottom and top of every cell using 3‑D‑printed screws; ensure top and bottom supports are aligned.

steps.title: Insert plastic tubes
steps.instruction: Fit the following plastic tubes into the tube supports:

substeps.instruction: 30 mm long tube (ID 9.525 mm, OD 12.7 mm) into each top support.
15 mm long tube (ID 9.525 mm, OD 12.7 mm) into each bottom support.
40 mm long tube (ID 6.35 mm, OD 9.525 mm) into each top tube.
20 mm long tube (ID 6.35 mm, OD 9.525 mm) into each bottom tube.
If tubes are warped, submerge the warped segment in boiling water for 1 min, straighten on a towel, let reach room temperature, then insert.

steps.title: Mount magnets in magnet supports
steps.instruction: Place two low‑friction neodymium magnets (10 mm diameter × 4 mm length, 2.22 kg holding force) into each magnet support, ensuring the pair repels, then lodge the inner tube into the support so gravity does not dislodge it.

steps.title: Assemble linear guide rails
steps.instruction: Slide two linear‑guide‑rail blocks into each rail, block openings facing upward, and lodge the rails upright into the windows on the outer vertical walls.

substeps.instruction: Secure each rail with:
‑ two short rail supports,
‑ two long rail supports,
‑ four M5 × 10 mm iron screws (0.8 thread, 5 mm diameter),
‑ two M5 × 20 mm iron screws (0.8 thread, 5 mm diameter),
‑ two M5 × 5 mm hex nuts.
If the rail becomes eroded, print and insert the T‑shaped peg from the 3D‑prints folder.

steps.title: Prepare flight‑arm axis
steps.instruction: Create the rotating arm axis using a 20 µL filtered pipette tip and a 19 G non‑magnetic hypodermic steel tube:

substeps.instruction: Puncture the filter of the pipette tip at its centre with an entomological pin and push the pin through until the steel ends protrude; the filter holds the pin in place.
Cut the steel tube to 24 cm (1 cm shorter than a flight cell).
Hot‑glue the protruding pin and the pipette‑tip crown to the tube’s midpoint.
Bend the tube 2 cm from the free end to a 95° angle.

steps.title: Test magnetic suspension of arm
steps.instruction: Place the assembled arm between the top set of magnets; verify that it spins freely around the vertically suspended pin.

steps.title: Add magnets and foil flag to arm
steps.instruction: Complete the pivot arm:

substeps.instruction: Glue two low‑friction neodymium magnets (3.05 mm diameter × 1.58 mm length, 0.23 kg holding force) onto the bent end of the arm (total arm mass with magnets ≈ 1.4 g).
Wrap a piece of aluminum foil (0.01 g cm⁻²) around the unbent end to form a flag; make the flag at least 3 mm wide (beam diameter ≤ 2.4 mm) to reliably interrupt the IR beam.

steps.title: Install IR sensors
steps.instruction: Place the IR‑sensor transmitter inside the top linear‑rail block with the emitter facing downwards, and the receiver inside the bottom block facing upwards.

substeps.instruction: Sensors are 20 mm × 10 mm × 8 mm; they may be spaced up to 250 mm apart (the rail is ≈ 100 mm).

steps.title: Wire sensors to data logger
steps.instruction: On a solderless breadboard, connect each sensor pair to a 4‑channel analog input data logger:

substeps.instruction: Connect the transmitter to the logger through a 180 Ω resistor.
Connect the receiver to the logger through a 2.2 kΩ resistor placed before the receiver output.
Arrange each channel in alternating rows to reduce noise.

steps.title: Run flight trials
steps.instruction: Test up to eight insects simultaneously; prepare at least sixteen insects (painted) for sequential testing.

substeps.instruction: Apply magnetic paint to each insect’s pronotum with a toothpick or 20 G precision tip; let dry ≥ 10 min (multiple layers optional).
Attach the painted insect to the arm magnets.
When an insect finishes, remove it, record its ID, chamber and set in datasheet.xlsx, and insert an event‑marker comment (see step 15).
After testing, chip off the magnetic paint with fine forceps and dispose of waste according to EPA and OSHA regulations.

steps.title: Set up WinDAQ software
steps.instruction: Install WinDAQ, create a folder structure, and configure acquisition:

substeps.instruction: Create folder Flight_scripts on the desktop with subfolders: data, files2split, recordings, split_files, standardized_files.
Copy datasheet.xlsx into the data folder.
Open WinDAQ Dashboard, select the desired data‑logger(s), and press “Start WinDAQ Software”.
Set Sample Rate to 100 samples / second (Edit → Sample Rate).
For each recording, choose File → Record, name the file with set number and channel letter (e.g., T1_set006-2-24-2020-B.txt), set the anticipated recording length, and start when insects are ready.
Terminate recording with Ctrl + S (only if needed).
To mark an insect change, select the channel, Edit → Insert Commented Mark, type the insect ID, and press OK.

steps.title: Export recordings
steps.instruction: Convert each .wdh file to a .txt CSV:

substeps.instruction: File → Save As, choose recordings folder, set file type to “Spreadsheet print (CSV)”, and add “.txt” extension.
In the options window, check Sample Rate, Relative Time, Date and Time, and Channel Number with Event Markers; set “1” between Channel Number and Event Markers; deselect all other options; click OK.

steps.title: Install Python environment
steps.instruction: Install Python 3.8.0 (or newer) and the libraries: csv, os, sys, re, datetime, time, numpy, math, matplotlib.

steps.title: Prepare datasheet for Python
steps.instruction: Open datasheet.xlsx and save it as CSV UTF‑8 (Windows) or CSV (Mac).

steps.title: Split recordings by insect
steps.instruction: Edit and run split_files.py:

substeps.instruction: If your filenames differ from the template, modify lines 133‑135 and 232‑233 accordingly.
Set the path to the Flight_scripts folder on line 266.
Run the script; it creates intermediate .txt files in files2split and per‑insect files in split_files.

steps.title: Standardize voltage troughs
steps.instruction: Edit and run standardize_troughs.py:

substeps.instruction: Set the Flight_scripts path on line 159.
Run the script; it writes standardized files (prefix “standardized_”) to standardized_files.
Open the generated trough_diagnostic.png and verify robustness.
If needed, uncomment line 198, set minimum and maximum deviation values (default 0.1 V), comment out line 189, and re‑run.

steps.title: Analyze flight statistics
steps.instruction: Edit and run flight_analysis.py:

substeps.instruction: Lines 76‑78: adjust optional speed‑correction threshold.
Line 121: set speed thresholds for unrealistic high/negative speeds.
Line 130: set time‑gap value to filter long pauses.
Line 350: set path to the folder containing the standardized *.txt files.
Line 353: input the arm radius used in the trials.
Lines 357‑358: set distance and time SI unit strings.
Lines 388‑397: ensure the split() function extracts insect ID, set number and chamber from the filename (e.g., standardized_T1_set006-2-24-2020-B.txt).
Run the script; it prints each insect’s ID, chamber and flight metrics and creates flight_stats_summary.csv in the data folder.
